subject: she

subject: they

subject: it

subject: I
learningHint: Use 'will' + base verb for the simple future. With the subject 'I' say 'I will go tomorrow.' Do not use 'will' + -ing (e.g., 'I will going') or the wrong subject form ('Me will go'). Note: 'They will go tomorrow.' is grammatically correct but uses a different subject.

subject: we

wrongAnswers: We will going to the park.
Her will be going to the park.
They will be went to the park.

Malayalam 'പോകുന്നിരിക്കും' matches the same 'will be going' idea.

subject: you
learningHint: 'Go' is irregular — its Simple Past form is 'went' for all subjects (I/you/he/she/we/they). For example, say 'You went home.' Do not use 'was' with 'went' or the base form 'go' when speaking about the past.

subject: he

subject: she
english: She could have been helping him.
wrongAnswers: Her was being able to help him.
We can have been helping him.
learningHint: Use 'could have been' + verb-ing to express a possible or hypothetical action that was ongoing in the past. Structure: subject + could have been + present participle (e.g., She + could have been + helping). Common mistakes: don't use object pronouns as subjects ('Her was...'), don't replace 'could' with 'can' for past possibility, and don't mix auxiliaries and tense (e.g., 'You could be helped him' is incorrect).

subject: they
learningHint: Use 'can' + base verb (solve). 'Can' does not change with the subject in the simple present, and you should not add -s to the main verb. For negatives use 'cannot' or 'can't' and for questions use 'Can they ...?'.

subject: it
english: It can be causing problems now.
wrongAnswers: They was being able to cause problems.
Me can be causing problems now.

subject: I
english: I will be able to help you tomorrow.
wrongAnswers: You can will help me tomorrow.
His will be able to help you tomorrow.
learningHint: Use 'will be able to' to express ability in the future — 'can' (present) becomes 'will be able to' (Simple Future). You can also use the contraction: "I'll be able to help you tomorrow."

subject: we
english: We can be helping them next week.
wrongAnswers: Their will be helping them next week.
I can be help them next week.
She could be helping they next week.

subject: you

subject: he

subject: she
learningHint: For past continuous with a singular third-person subject use 'was' + verb-ing: 'She was getting ready.' Do not use 'getted' — use 'getting'. Also watch subject–verb agreement (use 'were' with 'we', and 'his' is the wrong subject form).

subject: they
learningHint: In the simple present, use the base form 'get' with plural subjects like 'they' and 'we' (e.g., 'They get up early.'). For third-person singular (he/she/it) add -s: 'He gets up early.'

subject: it
learningHint: With singular third-person subjects (it/he/she) use 'is' + verb-ing: 'It is getting cold.' You can contract to 'It's getting cold.' The wrong answers fail subject-verb agreement ('you is'), use the base verb instead of -ing ('they are get'), or use the wrong pronoun form and omit the auxiliary ('me getting cold').

subject: I
english: I will get the book tomorrow.
wrongAnswers: we will gets the book tomorrow.
his will get the book tomorrow.
I going to get the book tomorrow.
learningHint: Form the simple future with 'will' + base verb: 'I will get...'. Do not add 's' to the verb (not 'gets'), use the correct subject (not 'his'), and if you choose 'going to' say 'I am going to get...'.

subject: we
english: We will be getting dinner at seven.
wrongAnswers: you will be get dinner at seven.
she will be getting dinner at sevened.
us will be getting dinner at seven.
learningHint: Use 'will be' + present participle (getting) for the future continuous: 'We will be getting dinner at seven.' You can also say the contraction 'We'll be getting...'. Common mistakes: do not use the base verb after 'will be' ('you will be get...'), do not add incorrect endings to time words ('sevend'), and use the subject pronoun 'we' (not 'us'). subject: you
english: You get a lot of emails.
wrongAnswers: their gets a lot of emails.
you getting a lot of emails.
he get a lot of emails.
learningHint: In Simple Present use the base verb with 'you': 'You get...' (not 'you gets'). 'Gets' is only for he/she/it. 'You getting...' is present continuous (needs 'are': 'You are getting...'). 'A lot of' means 'many'.

subject: he
learningHint: Use 'would' (the past form of 'will') in reported speech to show a future action from a past viewpoint. subject: she
english: She would be studying when I arrived.
wrongAnswers: We would studied when you came.
learningHint: Use 'would be + verb-ing' to show an action that was ongoing or expected at a past time (a future-in-the-past). Structure: subject + would + be + verb(-ing). Example: 'She would be studying when I arrived.' Common errors: wrong subject form ('his' → 'he'), wrong verb form after 'would' ('would studied' should be 'would be studying'), or missing -ing ('would be study' → 'would be studying').

subject: they
learningHint: Use 'would like' to express polite requests or preferences. Structure: subject + would like + noun (e.g. 'They would like some tea'). For questions: 'Would they like some tea?' subject: it
english: It would be raining now if the clouds were here.
malayalam: മേഘങ്ങൾ ഇവിടെ ഉണ്ടായിരുന്നെങ്കിൽ ഇനി മഴ പെയ്തിരിക്കമായിരിക്കും.
transliteration: meghangal ivide undayirunnengil ini mazha peythirikkumayirikkum.
learningHint: Use 'would be + verb-ing' to form a present unreal (hypothetical) continuous: 'It would be raining now if the clouds were here.' Common errors: wrong subject (me/they), missing auxiliary 'be' ('you would raining'), or using base verb instead of -ing ('would be rain').

subject: I
english: I would go tomorrow if I had time.
malayalam: എനിക്ക് സമയം ഉണ്ടായിരുന്നെങ്കിൽ ഞാൻ നാളെ പോവുമായിരിക്കും.

learningHint: This is a second conditional (hypothetical present/future). Use 'if' + past simple in the if-clause ('if I had time') and 'would' + base verb in the main clause ('would go'). 'Would' does not change with the subject; do not use 'would' with -ing or past participle forms (e.g., not 'would going' or 'would gone').

subject: we
english: We would be leaving at five tomorrow.
malayalam: ഞങ്ങൾ നാളെ അഞ്ച് മണിക്ക് പുറപ്പെടുകയാണ് ആയിരുന്നതായി പറയും.
transliteration: njangal nale anch manikku purappedukayaanayirunnathayi parayum.

me would be leaves at six.

Common errors: don't use the base verb after 'would' ('would be leave'), incorrect pronouns/forms ('me would be leaves'), or mix with past time words like 'yesterday' when talking about a future action.

subject: you
learningHint: Use 'would' + the base verb (prefer) to express a polite or conditional preference: 'You would prefer coffee.' Do not add -s or -ing to the main verb (not 'prefers' or 'preferring'), and use the correct subject (not 'their'). 'Would' does not change with different subjects.

subject: he

subject: she
learningHint: For the past continuous tense, use 'was' with 'she' + verb+ing: She was making tea. For the negative use 'wasn't' or 'was not' (She wasn't making tea).

subject: they

learningHint: In simple present use the base verb for plural subjects: 'they make' (not 'they makes'). 'Every night' indicates a habitual action. 'Made' is past tense, so it doesn't match the simple present.

subject: it
learningHint: For present continuous with a singular subject like 'it', use 'is' + verb‑ing: 'It is making a noise.' Avoid 'It make' (wrong) or 'They is' (subject-verb disagreement). 'Was making' would be past continuous.

subject: I

subject: we

wrongAnswers: We will making coffee in the morning.
Our will be making coffee in the morning.
We were be making coffee in the morning.
learningHint: Form the future continuous with 'will be' + verb-ing (present participle): 'We will be making coffee in the morning.' It describes an action that will be in progress at a future time. subject: you

He make your bed every morning.
You made your bed every morning.

subject: she

subject: they

subject: it

More natural English: 'It knows the password.' If you mean an ongoing action of acquiring the password, say 'It is learning the password.'

subject: I
learningHint: Use the simple future: 'will' + base verb. For example, 'I will know the result.' Do not add -s after 'will' ('will knows'), do not use 'Me' as the subject ('Me will...'), and do not use -ing after 'will' ('will knowing').

subject: we
english: We will be knowing the details tomorrow.
wrongAnswers: We will be know the details tomorrow.
us will be knowing the details.
She will be knowing the details tomorrowed.
learningHint: Use 'will be' + verb-ing for actions in progress at a future time (e.g., 'We will be studying at 7 pm'). The wrong answers show incorrect auxiliary or verb forms.

subject: you

wrongAnswers: Her was saying I will come.

subject: they
learningHint: Use 'will' + base verb to form the future (do not add '-s' to the verb). With 'they' say: 'They will come tomorrow.' 'Tomorrow' shows future time and commonly goes at the end of the sentence.

subject: it
english: It is saying it will stop.
wrongAnswers: They is saying it will stop.
You will be saying it stopped.

subject: I

subject: we

We will be went to the market.
Us will be going to the market.

subject: you
learningHint: This sentence uses 'will' + base verb to form the simple future: 'You will understand.' With the subject 'you' use 'will' (no -s on the main verb). Common errors add -s to the verb (e.g., 'understands') or change the subject incorrectly.

subject: he
wrongAnswers: I was think about the problem.
They will thinking about the problem.

subject: she
english: She was thinking about the problem.

wrongAnswers: His will think about the problem.

Yours is thinking it's a good idea.
He will think it's a good idea.

subject: it

We will be think about what to do next.

Her will be think about your proposal.

subject: you

subject: he

subject: she
learningHint: Form past continuous with subject + was/were + verb + -ing. For 'she' use 'was' and add -ing to 'take' → 'She was taking a photo.' Common errors: using the base verb ('He was take...'), wrong subject/auxiliary ('His were...'), or omitting the auxiliary ('They taking...').

subject: they
learningHint: In the simple present, plural subjects (they, we, you) use the base verb form: 'They take' (not 'They takes'). In Malayalam the plural subject 'അവർ (avar)' pairs with the verb ending '-കഴിക്കുന്നു (kazhikkunnu)'.

subject: it
english: It is taking longer than expected.
wrongAnswers: She is took longer than expected.
Their is taking longer than expected.

subject: I
english: I will take the train tomorrow.
wrongAnswers: I will taking the train tomorrow.
Her will take the train tomorrow.
We will took the train tomorrow.

subject: we

We will taking notes during the lecture.
They were be taking notes during the lecture.

subject: you

subject: he

subject: she

subject: they

subject: it

subject: I

subject: we

wrongAnswers: they will be saw the movie tomorrow.
me will be seeing the movie tomorrow.
her will seeing the movie tomorrow.

subject: you
learningHint: In simple present, use the base verb with you/I/we/they: 'You see the mistake.' Add -s only for third-person singular (he/she/it → 'sees'). 'It saw' is past tense. 'Their' is a possessive adjective — use 'they are' for present continuous ('they are seeing').

subject: he

subject: she

english: I should finish the report tomorrow.

I should finishes the report tomorrow.
They should finish tomorrow the report.
learningHint: Use 'should' + base verb to express advice, expectation, or mild obligation. Structure: subject + should + base verb (e.g., I should finish the report tomorrow). Do not add -s to the verb after 'should' (not 'finishes'), do not use 'me' as the subject, and keep the natural word order (report before time phrase or keep time phrase at end as in the example). The Malayalam 'poorthiyakkanam' conveys a similar sense of obligation/expectation.

subject: we
english: We should be meeting him next week.
wrongAnswers: His should be meeting him next week.
We should meeting him next week.
You should have been meeting him next week.
learningHint: Use 'should be' + present participle (-ing) to express expectation or a planned/likely action in the near future. In this sentence, 'We should be meeting him next week' means it's expected or arranged that we'll meet him. Common errors include omitting 'be' ('We should meeting...'), using the wrong subject ('His should...'), or using a past modal form ('should have been meeting') which refers to a past timeframe.

subject: you
learningHint: Use 'should' + base verb. With 'listen' use 'listen to' someone: 'You should listen to me.' Common mistakes: don't add -s to the verb ('listens'), don't drop 'to' after 'listen' ('listen me' is wrong), and watch the subject ('I should listen to me' is incorrect here).

subject: he
learningHint: Use the simple past form of the verb: 'call' → 'called'. Correct sentence: 'He called her yesterday.' Errors: 'She calling her yesterday.' should be 'She called her yesterday.' ('calling' is a present participle and needs an auxiliary to be correct); 'Me called her yesterday.' should be 'I called her yesterday.' (use subject pronoun); 'They was call her yesterday.' should be 'They called her yesterday.' (use correct past tense form and agreement).

subject: she
english: She was calling him when I arrived.
malayalam: ഞാൻ എത്തി യപ്പോൾ അവൾ അവനെ വിളിക്കുകയായിരുന്നു.
wrongAnswers: He was call him when I arrived.
They is calling him when I arrived.
learningHint: Use past continuous (was/were + verb+ing). For 'she' use 'was', so 'She was calling him'. Use past continuous for the ongoing/background action and simple past for the interrupting action: 'She was calling him when I arrived.' Common mistakes: using the base verb ('call') instead of 'calling', using the wrong auxiliary ('is'/'are'), or incorrect subject-verb agreement.

subject: they
english: They call their parents every Sunday.
malayalam: അവർ ഓരോ ഞായറാഴ്ചയും അവരുടെ മാതാപിതാക്കളെ വിളിക്കുന്നു.
transliteration: avar oro njayarazhchayum avarude mathapithakkale vilikkunnu.
wrongAnswers: I calls their parents every Sunday.
Their call their parents every Sunday.
She calling their parents every Sunday.
learningHint: This sentence describes a habitual action, so we use the simple present. With a plural subject like 'they' use the base form 'call' (not 'calls'). Place frequency words like 'every Sunday' after the verb phrase. Common errors: 'I calls' is wrong (say 'I call'), 'Their call' uses a possessive instead of the subject (use 'They call'), and 'She calling' is missing the correct verb form (use 'She calls' for simple present or 'She is calling' for present continuous).

subject: it
learningHint: Use 'is' with singular third-person subjects (he/she/it) and add -ing to the verb to form the present continuous: 'It is calling me.' Avoid forms like 'It call me' or 'They is calling me.'

subject: I
learningHint: Form the simple future with 'will' + base verb: 'I will call you tomorrow.' Use the subject 'I' (not 'me') and the base form 'call' (not 'calling'). In Malayalam, 'നാളെ' means 'tomorrow' and 'വിളിക്കും' (vilikkum) marks the future tense.

subject: we
english: We will be calling the clients next week.
wrongAnswers: We will be call the clients next week.
Their will be calling the clients next week.
He will calling the clients next week.
learningHint: Use 'will be' + verb-ing for actions that will be ongoing in the future. Example: 'We will be calling the clients next week.' You can contract 'We will' to 'We'll be calling...'. Avoid dropping 'be' ("will be call") or leaving out the -ing ("will calling") and watch subject words ("Their" is incorrect here).

subject: you
wrongAnswers: You was called me last night.
learningHint: Use the simple past form 'called' for the verb 'call'. In active sentences place the subject before the verb and the object after it: 'You called me last night.' Avoid forms like 'Me called...' or 'You was called...' which are incorrect in this context.

subject: he
english: He tried to open the door.
wrongAnswers: Me try to open the door yesterday.
They was trying to open the door.
learningHint: Use the simple past form 'tried' (note the spelling change y → i before adding -ed). With the subject 'he' say 'he tried' — not 'he try' or 'his tried'. Also avoid 'they was'; use 'they were' or 'they were trying' for past continuous.

subject: she
english: She was trying to fix the radio.
wrongAnswers: He were trying to fix the radio.
Us was trying to fix the radio.
She tryed to fixing the radio.
learningHint: Past continuous = subject + was/were + verb-ing. For 'she' use 'was': 'She was trying...'. The verb 'try' becomes 'trying' (not 'tryed'). Also avoid 'to' + '-ing' (e.g., 'to fixing'); use 'trying to fix' or 'was trying to fix' for an ongoing past action.

subject: they
wrongAnswers: They is trying new foods often.
learningHint: Use simple present for habits: 'They try new foods often.' With plural subjects (they) use the base verb 'try'. For third-person singular (he/she/it) change try → tries (consonant+y → ies). Adverb placement: 'They often try new foods.' or 'They try new foods often.'

subject: it
learningHint: Use present continuous: subject + am/is/are + verb+ing. With 'it' use 'is' → 'It is trying to start.' Avoid 'are' with 'it', avoid past tense 'tried' when you mean now, and don't use object pronoun 'her' as the subject (use 'she').

subject: I
learningHint: Use "will" + base verb: "I will try". Don't use the continuous form after "will" (not "will trying"). 'Tomorrow' shows future time and usually goes at the end. You can also use the contraction: "I'll try harder tomorrow."

subject: we
english: We will be trying the new method next week.
malayalam: ഞങ്ങൾ അടുത്ത ആഴ്ച പുതിയ രീതിയെ പരീക്ഷിക്കാൻ ശ്രമിച്ചുകൊണ്ടിരിക്കും.
transliteration: njaangal adutha aazhcha puthiya reethiye pareekshikkan shramichu konduirikkum.
wrongAnswers: We will trying the new method next week.
Us will be trying the new method next week.
They will be try the new method next week.
learningHint: Future continuous is formed with 'subject + will be + verb‑ing' (e.g., 'We will be trying...'). Common errors: 'We will trying...' omits 'be'; 'Us will be...' uses the wrong subject pronoun (use 'we'); 'They will be try...' uses the base verb instead of the '-ing' form.

subject: you
wrongAnswers: She is try to listen carefully.
learningHint: In the simple present, use the base form 'try' with subjects I/you/we/they (You try). For third-person singular (he/she/it) add -s: 'He tries'. Also use 'try' + 'to' + verb (try to listen), so 'She is try...' and 'Me try...' are incorrect.

subject: he
learningHint: In the simple past, use 'needed' for all subjects: 'He needed help.' Do not add -s in past tense (wrong: 'He needs help' for past). Also use the correct subject pronoun ('he', not 'me') and the correct past form ('needed', not 'is needed' or 'need'). In Malayalam: 'അവൻ സഹായം വേണ്ടിയിരുന്നു.' (avan sahayam vendiyirunnu.)

subject: she
learningHint: 'Need' is usually a stative verb and normally uses the simple past: 'She needed extra time.' The past continuous ('She was needing...') is uncommon and can sound unnatural; reserve continuous forms for rare cases emphasizing a temporary or developing need.

subject: they
learningHint: Use the base verb 'need' with the plural subject 'they' in the simple present: 'They need...'. 'Needs' is only for he/she/it. 'Me need...' is wrong because 'me' is an object pronoun (use 'I'). 'Their needs...' is possessive and changes the structure. 'We needing...' is ungrammatical without an auxiliary (use 'We need' or 'We are needing' if context requires).

subject: it
learningHint: 'Need' is usually a stative verb and not normally used in the continuous. Prefer: 'It needs repairs' or 'It is in need of repairs.' Note the third-person singular form uses 'needs'.

subject: I
learningHint: For simple future, use 'will' + base verb: 'I will need'. Do not use 'will' with '-ing' or past forms (avoid 'will needing' or 'will needed'), and use the correct subject ('I', not 'Us').

subject: we
english: We will be needing more time.
wrongAnswers: They will be need more time.
Her will be needing more time.
learningHint: Form the future continuous with 'will be' + verb-ing (present participle). Use 'We will be needing more time' to show an action that will be ongoing in the future. Common mistakes: omitting 'be' ('We will needing...') or using the base verb after 'will' ('They will be need...').

subject: you
wrongAnswers: You are needed to ask permission.
learningHint: In the simple past, 'need' becomes 'needed' and is followed by 'to' + base verb (needed to ask). For negatives/questions use 'didn't need to' and 'Did you need to...?'.

subject: he
learningHint: ‘Feel’ is irregular — its simple past is ‘felt’. Use the subject pronoun 'he' with the past form: 'He felt cold.' Avoid using object pronouns (e.g. 'her') as subjects, and make sure the verb tense matches time words (don’t use present 'feel' with past time like 'yesterday').

subject: she
learningHint: Past continuous = was/were + verb-ing. Use 'was' with singular third-person subjects (she/he/it), so 'she was feeling'. Make sure the verb is in -ing form ('feeling'), not base form ('feel'), and use the correct subject pronoun ('she' not 'her'). Also use 'were' (not 'was') with plural subjects like 'they'.

subject: they
learningHint: In the simple present use the base verb with plural subjects: 'they feel' (not 'they feels'). Do not add an auxiliary ('are') before the base verb in simple present. For third-person singular (he/she/it) add -s → 'he feels.'

subject: it
learningHint: Use the present continuous ('is feeling') for an ongoing or temporary sensation. Note: 'feel' is often a stative verb, so 'It feels soft.' is more common for general states. Also remember the auxiliary 'is' (not 'are') and the '-ing' form—e.g. correct: 'It is feeling soft.'; incorrect examples: 'It feeling soft.' (missing auxiliary), 'It are feeling soft.' (wrong auxiliary), 'He is feeling soft.' (wrong subject if you mean 'it').

subject: I
learningHint: Use 'will' + base verb to form the simple future: 'I will feel better.' Do not use '-ing' after 'will' (not 'I will feeling...'), do not use 'me' as the subject, and remember 'felt' is past tense. You can also contract 'I will' to 'I'll feel better.'

subject: we
learningHint: Future continuous = will be + verb-ing. Use 'will be feeling' (not 'will be feel'); 'will' is the same for all subjects. Example: 'We will be feeling tired.'

subject: you
learningHint: Use the base verb 'feel' with the subject 'you' in the Simple Present: 'You feel tired.' Don't say 'You are feel tired.' (if you use 'are', use the -ing form: 'You are feeling tired.'). 'Your feel tired.' is wrong because 'your' is a possessive adjective; use the subject 'you'. 'You felt tired.' is past tense, not Simple Present.

subject: he
learningHint: Tip: 'become' is irregular — the past simple form is 'became'. Use 'He became a teacher.' not 'He become...' or 'He was become.' Apply the same form for other subjects: 'I became', 'She became', 'They became'.

subject: she
learningHint: Past continuous = was/were + verb‑ing. For 'she' use 'was becoming' (gradual change). Do not use 'became' with 'was' (wrong: 'I was became') and avoid using a possessive ('his') as the subject—use 'he was becoming'. For plural subjects use 'were becoming' (e.g., 'They were becoming more confident').

subject: they
learningHint: In the simple present, plural subjects use the base verb: 'They become...'. For third-person singular (he/she/it) add -s: 'He becomes...'. Also use the correct subject pronoun (not 'Her' or 'Us') and do not add auxiliary verbs like 'was' in simple present.

subject: it
learningHint: Use 'is becoming' (am/is/are + becoming) to show an ongoing change in state. With the subject 'it' use 'is' (not 'they is'). The base form 'become' is not used alone in the present continuous—use the auxiliary verb + 'becoming' to emphasize the process of change. The Malayalam sentence reflects this ongoing change: 'ഇത് തണുത്തുപോകുകയാണ്.'

subject: I
learningHint: Use 'will' + base verb for simple future: 'I will become stronger.' You can use the contraction 'I'll become stronger.' Do not use 'became' (past) or omit 'will' when referring to the future.

subject: we
learningHint: Future continuous is formed with 'will be' + verb-ing. Here 'become' becomes 'becoming', so the correct sentence is 'We will be becoming leaders.' Avoid 'will becoming' (missing 'be') and 'will be became' (wrong verb form).

subject: you
malayalam: നീ ഒരു നല്ല സുഹൃത്ത് ആയി മാറി.
wrongAnswers: They was became a good friend.
learningHint: The simple past of the irregular verb 'become' is 'became'. With the subject 'you' use 'You became...' — not 'You become'. Also avoid using the possessive 'Yours' as the subject, and do not use 'was' with 'became' (e.g., not 'They was became').

subject: he
wrongAnswers: Me was leaving the office early.
they will leaving the office early.
learningHint: 'Leave' is irregular; the simple past form is 'left'. With subject 'he' use 'He left...'. The wrong answers show common errors: wrong pronoun ('Me'), incorrect possessive pronoun as subject ('his'), and wrong auxiliary/tense ('they will leaving'). Use 'left' for simple past statements.

subject: she
learningHint: Past continuous = subject + was/were + verb(-ing). For 'she' use 'was' + 'leaving' (She was leaving the room). Do not use the base verb 'leave' or incorrect subject-verb pairs like 'he was leave' or 'us were leaving'.

subject: they
english: They leave for work at eight.
malayalam: അവർ എട്ട് മണിക്ക് ജോലി പോകാൻ പുറപ്പെടുന്നു.
transliteration: avar ettu manikku joli pokan purappedunnu.
wrongAnswers: they leaving for work at eight.
her leaves for work at eight.
I leaves for work at eight.
learningHint: This is a simple present sentence showing a habitual action/schedule. With plural subjects like 'they' use the base verb 'leave' (no -s). For third-person singular use 'leaves' (he/she/it leaves). 'They leaving...' is incorrect; use 'They are leaving...' for present continuous.

subject: it
english: It is leaving a bad smell.
wrongAnswers: it are leaving a bad smell.
they is leaving a bad smell.
learningHint: Use 'is' with the singular third-person subject 'it' in present continuous: 'It is leaving a bad smell.' You may contract to 'It's leaving a bad smell.' Do not use 'it are', 'they is', or omit the apostrophe as in 'its leaving'.

subject: I
learningHint: Use 'will' + base verb for simple future: 'I will leave.' Do not use 'me' as the subject, do not add -ing after 'will' (not 'will leaving'), and do not use the past form 'left'. You can contract 'I will' to 'I'll' and place time expressions like 'tomorrow morning' at the end or start of the sentence.

subject: we
english: We will be leaving at noon.
wrongAnswers: us will be leaving at noon.
learningHint: Form the future continuous with 'will be' + verb-ing (present participle): 'We will be leaving at noon.' Common mistakes: 'we will leaving' (missing 'be'), 'us will be leaving' (wrong subject). 'We will leave' is simple future, not continuous.

subject: you
english: You leave your keys on the table.
wrongAnswers: you is leave your keys on the table.
yours leave your keys on the table.
you left your keys on the table.
learningHint: Tip: With 'you' in the simple present use the base verb form 'leave' (no -s). This sentence expresses a habitual action or present state. Word order: Subject + Verb + Object + Place. The Malayalam 'വയ്ക്കുന്നു' indicates present tense.

subject: he
english: He put the book on the shelf.
wrongAnswers: Her puts the book on the shelf.
They was put the book on shelf.
Me will putting the book on the shelf.
learningHint: Tip: 'put' is an irregular verb — base, simple past and past participle are all 'put'. For simple past use: Subject + put + object + (preposition phrase). Example: He put the book on the shelf. Note the preposition 'on' to show position.

subject: she
english: She was putting the plates on the table.
wrongAnswers: His put the plates on table.
We are put the plates on the table.
I will putting plates on the table.
learningHint: Past continuous uses was/were + verb-ing. For 'she' use 'was' → 'She was putting the plates on the table.' 'Put' becomes 'putting'. Avoid wrong pronoun-verb agreement and mixing tenses (e.g., 'His put...', 'We are put...', 'I will putting...').

subject: they
english: They put their shoes by the door.
malayalam: അവർ അവരുടെ ഷൂകൾ വാതिलിന് സമീപം വെക്കുന്നു.
transliteration: avar avarude shukal vaathilinu samipam vekkunnu.
wrongAnswers: You puts their shoes by door.
It were putting their shoes by the door.
Her will put their shoes by door.
learningHint: In the simple present with the plural subject 'they' use the base verb form 'put' (not 'puts'). Note: 'put' is the same in present and past. 'By the door' describes the location (near the door).

subject: it
english: It is putting the plug into the socket.
wrongAnswers: Us is putting the plug into socket.
She puting the plug into the socket.
They will be put the plug into the socket.
learningHint: Use 'is' with the singular subject 'it' for present continuous: 'It is ...'. The verb 'put' becomes 'putting' (note the double 't'). Watch for wrong pronouns, missing doubled consonants ('puting'), and incorrect tense/word order ('They will be put the...').

subject: I
english: I will put the keys on the table.
wrongAnswers: He will putting the keys on the table.
Their put the keys on table.
You will be put the keys on the table.
learningHint: For simple future use 'will' + the base verb: 'I will put...'. Do not use the -ing form after 'will' (not 'will putting'). Include articles for places ('on the table', not 'on table'), and use the correct subject and active form ('I will put', not 'Their put' or 'You will be put').

subject: we
english: We will be putting the decorations up tomorrow.
wrongAnswers: His will puting the decorations up tomorrow.
Me are putting decorations up tomorrow.
They will putting the decorations up tomorrow.
learningHint: Structure: subject + 'will be' + verb-ing. Use 'will be putting' to show an action that will be in progress in the future. Common mistakes: omitting 'be' after 'will' ("will putting"), using the wrong subject form ("me", "his"), or wrong verb endings. Correct: "We will be putting the decorations up tomorrow."

subject: you
english: You put sugar in your tea.
wrongAnswers: I puts sugar in your tea.
Her is putting sugar in your tea.
They will put sugar in you tea.
learningHint: In the simple present with 'you' use the base verb 'put' (not 'puts'). Also use correct pronouns and possessives: use subject pronouns like 'she' (not 'her') in subject position — e.g., 'She is putting...'; and use 'your' before a noun — e.g., 'your tea' (not 'you tea').

subject: he
learningHint: Note: 'mean' is irregular — the past tense is 'meant' for all subjects (He meant, They meant). Use the correct subject pronoun ('he' not 'her' or 'me'). Do not form the past by adding -ed ('meaned' is incorrect). Also, 'They was meaning well.' is ungrammatical ('were' would be used for past continuous), but the natural simple past is 'They meant well.'

subject: she
english: She was meaning to call him.
wrongAnswers: his was meaning to call him.
Me were meaning to call him.
learningHint: Although 'mean' is usually a stative verb, the form 'be meaning to' (as in 'She was meaning to call him.') is used to express an ongoing intention or plan in the past. In many situations the simple past 'She meant to call him.' is more common, but use 'was meaning to' to emphasize the intention was in progress or to introduce a polite explanation (e.g. 'I was meaning to ask you...').

subject: they
learningHint: 'They mean well.' = 'They have good intentions.' Note subject-verb agreement: use 'mean' with 'they' and 'you' (not 'means'); use 'means' with he/she/it (e.g., 'He means well.'). The past is 'meant' (not 'meaned'). 'Mean' can also mean 'be unkind', but in this phrase it means 'intend to be kind.'

subject: it
english: It is meaning the same thing.
wrongAnswers: their is meaning the same thing.
We was meaning the same thing.
learningHint: Use the simple present: say 'It means the same thing.' 'Mean' is usually a stative verb, so avoid 'is meaning' in this context. The listed wrong answers show wrong pronoun ('their'), missing auxiliary, and incorrect subject-verb agreement ('We was').

subject: I
english: I will mean what I say.
wrongAnswers: you will mean what I say.
I will meaning what I say.
his will mean what he say.
learningHint: Use the base verb after 'will': say 'I will mean' (not 'I will meaning'). Also correct subject form for third person is 'He will mean' (not 'his will mean'). Here 'mean' = 'intend' — you can use the contraction 'I'll mean'. Practice by changing the subject while keeping the base verb: 'You will mean...', 'We will mean...'.

subject: we
english: We will be meaning the same thing.
wrongAnswers: us will be meaning the same thing.
We will meaning the same thing.
they will been meaning the same thing.
learningHint: Form the future continuous with 'will be' + verb-ing (e.g., 'We will be meeting'). Note common errors: don't use 'us' as the subject, don't drop 'be' ('We will meaning...' is wrong), and don't use 'been' after 'will' ('will been' is wrong). Also remember that 'mean' is often a stative verb and is usually used in simple future ('We will mean the same thing') rather than continuous.

subject: you
english: You mean a lot to me.
wrongAnswers: your mean a lot to me.
You meant a lot to me.
They meaned a lot to me.
learningHint: Use the base verb 'mean' with the subject 'you' in simple present. Don't confuse 'you' (subject) with 'your' (possessive). The past form is 'meant' (not 'meaned'), and third-person singular (he/she/it) takes 'means'.

subject: he
learningHint: Tip: 'keep' is irregular — its simple past form is 'kept'. In the simple past the verb form does not change with the subject, so 'He kept the promise.' is correct. Watch pronouns and verb forms: 'Her keep...' uses the wrong pronoun and verb, 'They keeps...' has the wrong verb form, and 'Me kept...' uses the wrong subject pronoun.

subject: she
english: She was keeping the door closed.
wrongAnswers: His was keeping the door closed.
Me was keeping the door closed.
learningHint: For past continuous with third-person singular use 'was' + verb-ing: 'She was keeping...'. 'Keeping the door closed' means maintaining that state; the wrong answers show incorrect subject-verb agreement or wrong past continuous formation.

subject: they
learningHint: With plural subjects like 'they' in the simple present, use the base form of the verb: 'They keep...'. Do not add -s (They keeps) or use object pronouns (Them keep).

subject: it
english: It is keeping the files safe.
wrongAnswers: You is keeping the files safe.
learningHint: Use the correct form of the verb 'to be' + verb-ing for present continuous. For the singular subject 'it' use 'is' → 'It is keeping the files safe.' Common mistakes shown: 'You is...' should be 'You are...'; 'We kept...' is past simple, not present continuous; 'Her is...' is incorrect subject/pronoun — use 'She is...'.

subject: I
english: I will keep the keys with me.
wrongAnswers: He will keep the keys with me.
I keep the keys with me tomorrow.
Our will keep the keys with me.
learningHint: Form the simple future with 'will' + base verb: 'I will keep the keys with me.' You can also use the contraction 'I'll keep...'. Ensure the subject matches the verb (don't change 'I' to 'He' or 'Our'), and avoid using present simple ('I keep... tomorrow') to express future time.

subject: we
english: We will be keeping the windows closed.
wrongAnswers: They will be keeping the windows closed.
We keep the windows closed tomorrow.
Me will be keeping windows closed.
learningHint: Future continuous = subject + will be + verb‑ing. Use it to describe an action that will be in progress at a specific time in the future (e.g., "At noon tomorrow, we will be keeping the windows closed"). Note also that "keep" can take an object plus an adjective ("keep the windows closed"). Avoid changing the subject ("They will...") or using incorrect pronouns ("Me will...") or the simple present for a planned future time ("We keep... tomorrow").

subject: you
english: You keep the door locked at night.
wrongAnswers: Yours keep the door locked at night.
You keeps the door locked at night.
They keep the door locked at night.
learningHint: In the simple present we use 'keep' with I/you/we/they and 'keeps' with he/she/it. The simple present often describes habits or routines (e.g., "You keep the door locked at night"). Form questions and negatives with 'do': "Do you keep the door locked at night?" / "You do not (don't) keep the door locked at night."

subject: he
learningHint: Use the pattern: subject + let + object + base verb (He let me go). 'Let' does not change in the past tense (past = let). It means 'allow'; common mistakes are using 'letted' or the wrong object pronoun (say 'me', not 'I').

subject: she
english: She was letting the children play outside.
learningHint: Use 'was/were letting' to describe an ongoing act of allowing in the past. With a singular subject like 'she' use 'was letting'. Structure: [subject] + was/were + letting + object + verb‑ing. Example: "She was letting the children play outside."

subject: they
english: They let their dog run in the park.
malayalam: അവർ അവരുടെ നായയെ പാർക്കിൽ ഓടാൻ അനുവദിക്കുന്നു.
transliteration: avar avarute naaye paarkkil odan anuvadikkunnu.
wrongAnswers: we letting the dog in park.
his let the dog to run.
learningHint: Use 'let' unchanged in the simple present for all subjects. After 'let' use the base verb (no 'to'): e.g. 'They let their dog run in the park.' Common mistakes: adding -s ('I lets...'), using progressive form ('we letting...'), or adding 'to' after 'let' ('let the dog to run').

subject: it
english: It is letting the water flow.
wrongAnswers: I will be let it flow.
learningHint: Use 'is letting' for an ongoing action with the third-person singular subject 'it' (subject + is/are/am + verb-ing). After 'let' use the base verb without 'to' (let the water flow). Also check subject-verb agreement (e.g., 'you are', 'they are') and avoid incorrect passive or extra‑word constructions like 'I will be let it flow.'

subject: I
